question:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them may contain an error. Select the part that contains the error from the given options. If you don’t find any error, mark ‘No error’ as your answer.
Neither my brother nor my brothers-in-law / attended the meeting / as his health is not more good.
option_1: Neither my brother nor my brothers-in-law
option_4: as his health is not more good
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. as his health is not more good.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrase "is not more good" is grammatically incorrect. "More" is used to form the comparative degree of long/polysyllabic adjectives (e.g., more beautiful, more careful), but "good" already has its own comparative and superlative forms — better and best — and cannot take "more" before it.

• Rule: Irregular adjectives like good, bad, little, many/much form comparatives irregularly (good → better → best) and are never preceded by "more" or "most".

• The correct phrasing would be "as his health is not very good" or "as his health is no better", not "is not more good".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Neither my brother nor my brothers-in-law" is correct. With "neither...nor", the verb agrees with the subject nearer to it (here, "brothers-in-law"), and since the main verb "attended" is in the simple past tense, it does not change for number, so this part is free of error.

• Option 2: "attended the meeting" is correct. The simple past tense form "attended" correctly reports a completed past action; there is no error of tense or form here.

• Option 3: "No error" is incorrect as an answer because an error does exist in the sentence (in part 4), so "No error" cannot be selected.

NOTE

• Common irregular comparatives frequently tested by SSC: good – better – best; bad – worse – worst; little – less – least; many/much – more – most; far – farther/further – farthest/furthest.

• Never use "more" or "most" together with an adjective that already has an irregular comparative/superlative form (avoid "more better", "most best", "more worse", etc.).

question:
Parts of a sentence are given below in jumbled order. Select the option that arranges the parts in the correct sequence to form a meaningful sentence.
(P) kindness and empathy
(Q) in a world that can be
(O) bring light and positivity
(R) harsh and challenging
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. QRPO.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct sequence is: (Q) in a world that can be (R) harsh and challenging (P) kindness and empathy (O) bring light and positivity, forming the sentence: "In a world that can be harsh and challenging, kindness and empathy bring light and positivity."

• Q must come first because it introduces the setting ("in a world that can be..."), which needs a completing adjective.

• R ("harsh and challenging") logically follows Q, completing the description of the kind of world being spoken of.

• P ("kindness and empathy") then introduces the subject of the main clause, and O ("bring light and positivity") supplies the verb and object that complete the sentence meaningfully.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: PORQ is incorrect because it places "kindness and empathy" (P) at the start without the introductory context of "in a world that can be" (Q), and ends with "in a world that can be" (Q), leaving the sentence without a completing adjective.

• Option 2: ROQP is incorrect because it begins with "harsh and challenging" (R) with no subject or context to attach to, producing a meaningless opening.

• Option 4: QROP is incorrect because it reverses the order of P and O at the end, giving "harsh and challenging bring light and positivity kindness and empathy," which is grammatically and logically broken.

NOTE

• In parajumble/sentence-rearrangement questions, always look first for the part that can logically stand as the opening (often one with a clear subject or an introductory phrase) and the part that provides a natural conclusion.

• Watch for grammatical clues like articles, pronouns, and conjunctions ("that can be", "and") which signal which parts must be adjacent.

question:
Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word from the given sentence .
She recieved an award for her outstanding performance.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. recieved.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "received", not "recieved".

• Spelling rule — "i before e except after c": When the sound is a long "ee" sound, the rule is "i before e except after c". Since the letter before "ie/ei" here is "c", the correct order is "ei", giving rec-EI-ved, not "rec-IE-ved".

• Example: She received an award for her outstanding performance. (correct spelling)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "award" is spelt correctly; it means a prize or recognition given for achievement.

• Option 3: "performance" is spelt correctly; it refers to how well a task or role is carried out.

• Option 4: "outstanding" is spelt correctly; it means exceptionally good or remarkable.

NOTE

• The "i before e except after c" rule applies to words with a long "ee" sound: believe, achieve, niece (i before e) vs. receive, deceive, ceiling, perceive (e before i, after c).

• Common exceptions to memorise separately: seize, weird, either, neither, science, species.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
To read between the lines
option_4: To understand more than what the words suggest
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. To understand more than what the words suggest.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "To read between the lines" means to understand the hidden or implied meaning of something, beyond what is literally or explicitly stated. (शब्दों के पीछे छिपे अर्थ को समझना)
◦ Example: He didn't say he was upset, but if you read between the lines, you could tell something was wrong.

• The expression originates from a method of writing secret messages between the visible lines of a text using invisible ink, so that the "real" message lay hidden between the printed lines.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: To underline some words (कुछ शब्दों को रेखांकित करना): This refers to literally marking words, which is unrelated to inferring hidden meaning.

• Option 2: To read differently (अलग ढंग से पढ़ना): This is a vague, literal notion of varying one's reading style and does not capture the idiom's sense of inference.

• Option 3: To read aloud to public (जनता के सामने ज़ोर से पढ़ना): This describes public recitation, which has nothing to do with interpreting implied meaning.

NOTE

• Other idioms of hidden/implied meaning often asked in SSC: "To read someone like a book" (to understand someone completely), "To hit the nail on the head" (to describe exactly what is causing a situation), and "To beat around the bush" (to avoid the main point).

question:
Select the word OPPOSITE in meaning to the given word.
Deficient
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Ample.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Deficient" means lacking in some necessary quality or element; insufficient. (अपर्याप्त, कमी वाला) Its opposite is "Ample", meaning more than sufficient; plentiful. (पर्याप्त, प्रचुर)
◦ Example: Unlike his deficient earlier draft, his revised essay showed ample evidence of careful research.

• Rule: For antonym questions, first fix the precise sense of the given word — here "deficient" relates to quantity/sufficiency, not to physical condition — and choose the option that opposes that specific sense.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Skimpy" (अपर्याप्त, तंग): Means scanty or barely sufficient — this is actually close in meaning to "deficient", not its opposite.

• Option 2: "Broken" (टूटा हुआ): Means damaged or not working, describing physical condition rather than sufficiency, so it is not the antonym of "deficient".

• Option 4: "Terrible" (भयानक, बहुत ख़राब): Means extremely bad or unpleasant; this is a general negative quality word, not related to the idea of quantity/sufficiency.

NOTE

• Words related in meaning to "deficient": inadequate, insufficient, scanty, meagre, lacking.

• Words related in meaning to "ample": abundant, plentiful, copious, sufficient, adequate.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Meander
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Direct.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Meander" means to follow a winding, indirect course, especially of a path, river, or conversation. (घुमावदार रास्ते से चलना) Its opposite is "Direct", meaning to go straight to a place or point, without turning or wandering. (सीधे जाना)
◦ Example: Instead of meandering through side topics, he went direct to the main point.

• Rule: In antonym questions involving movement or path-related words, check whether the given word implies a "winding/indirect" sense or a "straight/direct" one, and pick the option that expresses the opposite sense.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Ramble" (बेमतलब घूमना/बातें करना): Means to wander aimlessly or talk at length without a clear purpose — this is a near-synonym of "meander", not its opposite.

• Option 2: "Deputise" (प्रतिनिधि नियुक्त करना): Means to appoint someone to act on one's behalf; it is unrelated in meaning to "meander" or "direct".

• Option 3: "Confirm" (पुष्टि करना): Means to establish the truth of something; it has no connection with the idea of a winding versus straight course.

NOTE

• Synonyms of "meander": wind, wander, snake, zigzag, ramble.

• Synonyms of "direct" (in this sense): straight, undeviating, unswerving, straightforward.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word in the following sentence.
In Shakespeare’s The Merchant of Venice, Shylock’s connivance aimed to jeopardise Antonio’s life.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Safeguard.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Jeopardise" means to put someone or something into a situation of danger, risk, or harm. (ख़तरे में डालना) Its opposite is "Safeguard", meaning to protect from harm or danger. (सुरक्षा प्रदान करना)
◦ Example: Shylock's connivance aimed to jeopardise Antonio's life, but the court intervened to safeguard it.

• Rule: For antonym questions on underlined words in a sentence, first paraphrase the underlined word in context — here "aimed to jeopardise Antonio's life" means "aimed to endanger" his life — then find the option opposite to that sense.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Risk" (जोख़िम): Means exposure to danger or harm — this is a near-synonym of "jeopardise", not its opposite.

• Option 3: "Peril" (संकट, खतरा): Means serious and immediate danger — again a synonym of "jeopardise", not an antonym.

• Option 4: "Jape" (मज़ाक, हंसी-मज़ाक): Means a practical joke or prank; it is unrelated in meaning to either "jeopardise" or "safeguard".

NOTE

• Synonyms of "jeopardise": endanger, imperil, risk, threaten, compromise.

• Synonyms of "safeguard": protect, shield, defend, secure, preserve.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
Two of the fugitives managed to remain free by adeptly avoiding the_____________ of the police.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. pursuit.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Pursuit" means the act of chasing or following someone in order to catch them, which fits the context of fugitives avoiding being chased and caught by the police.

• Rule: In sentence-completion questions, the chosen word must fit both the grammatical structure and the precise logical context — here, fugitives who "remain free" would specifically be avoiding being "chased"/"pursued", not merely being "found", "restricted", or "followed" in a general sense.

• Applying the rule: "avoiding the pursuit of the police" correctly conveys that the fugitives evaded being chased down.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "following" is incorrect because "the following of the police" does not idiomatically express the sense of being chased; "following" more naturally describes a group of supporters or a subsequent event.

• Option 2: "repression" is incorrect because "repression" means forceful suppression or restraint of a group/emotion, which does not fit the specific act of evading capture.

• Option 4: "discovery" is incorrect because "discovery" refers to finding something for the first time, not the ongoing act of chasing; fugitives evade the "pursuit", not merely the "discovery," of the police.

NOTE

• Words related to "pursuit" often tested by SSC: chase, hunt, quest.

• Commonly confused pair: "pursuit" (chasing to catch) vs. "persuasion" (convincing someone) — do not mix these up in fill-in-the-blank questions.

question: Select the correctly spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Conscientious.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Conscientious" — meaning wishing to do one's work or duty well and thoroughly.
◦ Example: She is a conscientious student who always completes her assignments on time.

• Spelling key: CON + SCI + ENTI + OUS. Note the sequence "sci" (as in "science"), followed by "enti", and the ending "-ous".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Conscientous" — incorrect; the "i" before "ous" has been dropped (should be "-entious", not "-entous").

• Option 2: "Conscencious" — incorrect; "sci" has been wrongly written as "sce" and the internal sequence is disturbed.

• Option 4: "Conscietious" — incorrect; the "n" after "sci" has been dropped ("Consci-" wrongly written as "Consci-e" without the "n").

NOTE

• Related words with the "sci" root often confused in spelling: science, conscious, conscience, omniscient.

• Commonly confused pair: "conscious" (aware) vs. "conscientious" (diligent, dutiful) — different meanings despite similar spelling.

question:
Select the option that can replace the underlined phrase and make the sentence grammatically correct.
The programme on TV was now shown the blurring faces of the inmates of the rehabilitation centre .
option_1: were now showing the blurred faces of the inmates of the rehabilitation centre.
option_2: was now showing the blurred faces of the inmates of the rehabilitation centre
option_3: were now showing the blurring faces of the inmates from the rehabilitation centre
option_4: was now showing the blurred faces of the inmates upon the rehabilitation centre
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. was now showing the blurred faces of the inmates of the rehabilitation centre.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The original sentence "The programme on TV was now shown the blurring faces..." contains two errors: (i) the passive construction "was shown" is illogical here because a programme cannot logically be "shown" its own faces — the programme is itself the agent doing the showing, so the active/continuous form "was showing" is required; and (ii) "blurring" (present participle, meaning "in the act of blurring") is the wrong form — the faces have already been deliberately blurred, so the past participle "blurred" (meaning "made blurred") is required.

• Rule — participle usage: Use the present participle (-ing form) for something actively performing an action, and the past participle (-ed/-en form) for something that has had an action done to it. Here, the faces did not blur themselves; they were blurred by an editor, so "blurred" (passive/completed sense) is correct, not "blurring".

• Applying both corrections together: "The programme on TV was now showing the blurred faces of the inmates of the rehabilitation centre" is the grammatically correct version, keeping "of the rehabilitation centre" unchanged.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "were now showing..." is incorrect because the subject "The programme" is singular, so it must take the singular auxiliary "was", not the plural "were".

• Option 3: "were now showing the blurring faces...from the rehabilitation centre" is incorrect on two counts: it wrongly uses "were" with the singular subject, and it retains the incorrect present participle "blurring" instead of "blurred".

• Option 4: "was now showing the blurred faces...upon the rehabilitation centre" is incorrect because the preposition "upon" is wrong here; the correct preposition is "of" ("the inmates of the rehabilitation centre"), showing possession/association, not "upon".

NOTE

• Commonly confused participle pairs tested by SSC: blurring/blurred, boring/bored, exciting/excited, interesting/interested — the "-ing" form describes the doer/cause, the "-ed" form describes the receiver/experiencer of the feeling or action.

• Watch subject-verb agreement with "was/were" carefully whenever the subject is a singular collective noun like "programme", "team", or "committee".

question:
Given below are four jumbled sentences. Select the option that gives their correct logical sequence.
A. It contains high levels of Vitamin A and D.
B. Cod liver oil is thus used to treat arthritis.
C. This supplement is made from the liver of cod fish.
D. Cod liver oil is a nutritional supplement.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. DCAB.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct sequence is: (D) Cod liver oil is a nutritional supplement. (C) This supplement is made from the liver of cod fish. (A) It contains high levels of Vitamin A and D. (B) Cod liver oil is thus used to treat arthritis.

• D must come first because it introduces the topic, "cod liver oil," in general terms as a nutritional supplement.

• C logically follows D because it explains what the supplement (referred to as "this supplement") is made from, directly picking up the noun introduced in D.

• A then follows, describing a specific property (high Vitamin A and D content) of the supplement described in C, and B concludes with the resulting use ("thus used to treat arthritis"), which follows logically from the vitamin content mentioned in A.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: ABCD is incorrect because it opens with "It contains high levels of Vitamin A and D," but the pronoun "It" has no preceding noun to refer to, making the opening unclear.

• Option 2: CBAD is incorrect because it opens with "This supplement," but the noun "supplement" is not yet introduced, so "This" has nothing to point back to.

• Option 4: BACD is incorrect because it opens with "Cod liver oil is thus used to treat arthritis," using the conclusion-word "thus" before any supporting reasoning has been given.

NOTE

• In logical-sequencing questions, look for pronouns ("it", "this", "these") that require an antecedent noun earlier in the sequence, and for conclusion markers ("thus", "therefore", "hence") that must come only after the supporting facts.

• The sentence introducing the general topic (here, naming "cod liver oil" as a supplement) almost always opens the sequence.

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
A person who is trained to travel in a spacecraft.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Astronaut.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Astronaut" means a person who is trained to travel and work in a spacecraft. (अंतरिक्ष यात्री)
◦ Example: The astronaut spent six months aboard the space station conducting experiments.

• The word is formed from the Greek roots "astro-" (star) and "-naut" (sailor), literally meaning "star sailor".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Anthropologist" (मानवविज्ञानी): A person who studies human societies, cultures, and their development — unrelated to space travel.

• Option 3: "Alchemist" (कीमियागर): A person who practised alchemy, an early form of chemistry aimed at transforming base metals into gold — unrelated to space travel.

• Option 4: "Curator" (संग्रहाध्यक्ष): A person who manages or looks after a museum, gallery, or collection — unrelated to space travel.

NOTE

• Related one-word substitutions often tested by SSC: Cosmonaut (a Russian astronaut), Aviator (a pilot of an aircraft), Navigator (one who plans and directs the course of a ship or aircraft).

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Merit
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Virtue.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Merit" means a good quality or worth that deserves praise or reward. (गुण, योग्यता) "Virtue" means a good or admirable quality; moral excellence. (सद्गुण), making it the closest synonym.
◦ Example: Patience is considered a great merit/virtue in a teacher.

• Rule: For synonym questions, identify the core sense of the given word — here "merit" refers to a positive, praiseworthy quality — and match it with the option carrying the same core sense.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Fatigue" (थकान): Means extreme tiredness, an unrelated sense to "a good quality".

• Option 2: "Oblique" (तिरछा, अप्रत्यक्ष): Means slanting, or indirect (as in speech); unrelated to "merit".

• Option 4: "Residue" (अवशेष): Means the remainder left after a process is complete; unrelated to "merit".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "merit": worth, excellence, quality, credit, distinction.

• Do not confuse "merit" (a good quality) with "demerit" (a fault or disadvantage) — they are antonyms, not variants.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Jovial
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Cheerful.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Jovial" means friendly, cheerful, and full of good humour. (हंसमुख, आनंदी) "Cheerful" carries the same sense of being noticeably happy and good-humoured. (प्रसन्नचित्त)
◦ Example: Despite the long queue, the jovial/cheerful shopkeeper kept everyone smiling with his jokes.

• Rule: For synonym questions on words describing temperament, isolate whether the word conveys a positive or negative mood, then match with an option of the same emotional charge — "jovial" is clearly positive.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Miserable" (दुखी): Means extremely unhappy — the opposite emotional charge to "jovial".

• Option 2: "Solemnity" (गंभीरता): A noun meaning seriousness or solemn behaviour; besides being the wrong part of speech, it is nearly opposite in tone to "jovial".

• Option 4: "Profane" (अपवित्र, अशिष्ट): Means showing disrespect for sacred things, or vulgar/coarse in language; unrelated to "jovial".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "jovial": jolly, merry, genial, convivial, good-humoured.

• Commonly confused antonym: "jovial" vs. "sullen"/"morose" (bad-tempered, gloomy).

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.
Each candidate was making tall promises.
option_1: Tall promises were being made by each candidate.
option_2: Tall promises are made by each candidate.
option_3: Tall promises will be made by each candidate.
option_4: Tall promises are being made by each candidate.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Tall promises were being made by each candidate.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "Each candidate was making tall promises" is in the Past Continuous Tense.

• Rule — Past Continuous Tense:
◦ Active: Subject + was/were + V1+ing + Object
◦ Passive: Object + was/were + being + V3 + by + Subject

• Applying the rule: the object "tall promises" becomes the subject; being plural, it takes "were"; the auxiliary structure adds "being"; the verb "making" becomes the past participle "made"; and "each candidate" becomes the agent with "by".
◦ Passive: Tall promises were being made by each candidate.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 is incorrect because "are made" is the passive of the Simple Present Tense, not the Past Continuous Tense of the original sentence.

• Option 3 is incorrect because "will be made" is the passive of the Simple Future Tense, which changes the time frame of the original sentence.

• Option 4 is incorrect because "are being made" is the passive of the Present Continuous Tense, not the Past Continuous Tense required here.

NOTE

• A quick way to identify the correct tense in passive-voice questions is to first name the tense of the active sentence accurately, and then apply only that tense's fixed passive formula.

• Past Continuous passive always uses "was/were + being + V3" — never drop the "being", as doing so would produce the Simple Past passive instead.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
Jump the gun
option_4: To do something too soon and too quickly
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. To do something too soon and too quickly.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Jump the gun" means to act before the proper or appropriate time, especially hastily and without adequate thought or preparation. (समय से पहले जल्दबाज़ी में कुछ करना)
◦ Example: He jumped the gun by announcing the result before the official confirmation arrived.

• The expression comes from athletics, where a runner who starts running before the starter's gun is fired is said to have "jumped the gun" — that is, started too early.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: To start all over again (फिर से शुरू करना): Means to restart something from the beginning, which is unrelated to acting prematurely.

• Option 2: Using a gun for sports (खेल में बंदूक का उपयोग करना): This is a literal, unrelated interpretation of the words "gun", not the idiomatic sense.

• Option 3: To stop a process (किसी प्रक्रिया को रोकना): Means to halt something, which is the opposite of "acting hastily/prematurely" and is unrelated to the idiom's meaning.

NOTE

• Other idioms of premature/hasty action often asked in SSC: "To put the cart before the horse" (to do things in the wrong order), "To count one's chickens before they hatch" (to assume success before it is certain).

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the underlined word in the given sentence.
Layla is the Sultan’s consort.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Partner.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Consort" (used as a noun, as here) means a husband or wife, especially of a reigning monarch; a companion or partner. (जीवनसाथी, साथी) "Partner" carries the same core sense of a companion/spouse. (साथी, जीवनसाथी)
◦ Example: Layla is the Sultan's consort/partner, and she often accompanies him at state functions.

• Rule: In synonym questions with an underlined word, first check the word's part of speech and context — here "consort" is used as a noun meaning "spouse/companion" (not the verb "to consort with", meaning to associate with) — and match accordingly.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Foe" (शत्रु): Means an enemy or opponent, the opposite sense of a close companion.

• Option 2: "Alcoholic" (शराबी): Means a person addicted to alcohol; entirely unrelated to "consort".

• Option 3: "Enemy" (शत्रु): Like "foe", means an adversary, the opposite of a close companion/spouse.

NOTE

• "Consort" as a verb (e.g., "to consort with criminals") means to associate or keep company with, usually in a negative context — do not confuse this with the noun sense of "spouse/companion" used here.

• Other royal-family-related vocabulary tested by SSC: regent (one who rules on behalf of a monarch), heir apparent, abdicate (to give up the throne).

question:
Parts of the following sentence have been given as options. Select the option that contains an error.
Rahul thinks he is as smarter as his friends in the class.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. he is as smarter as.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrase "as smarter as" is grammatically incorrect. The construction "as...as" is used to show equality between two things and must be followed by the positive degree of the adjective, not the comparative degree.

• Rule — as + positive degree + as: Use "as + adjective (positive form) + as" to compare two equal things (e.g., "as smart as", "as tall as"). Never use the comparative form ("-er"/"more") inside this structure.

• The correct phrasing is "he is as smart as his friends", not "he is as smarter as his friends".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "his friends" is correct; it is simply the noun phrase being compared to, with no grammatical error.

• Option 3: "Rahul thinks" is correct; it is a straightforward subject-verb combination in the simple present tense, correctly introducing the reported thought.

• Option 4: "in the class" is correct; it is a grammatically sound prepositional phrase specifying the location/group being referred to.

NOTE

• Common error pattern tested by SSC: mixing "as...as" (equality) with a comparative adjective, e.g., "as bigger as", "as taller as" — always correct these to the positive degree: "as big as", "as tall as".

• Contrast with genuine comparatives, which use "than", not "as...as": "He is smarter than his friends" (correct use of comparative).

question:
In the given question, a statement divided into different segments is given. Rearrange all the segments to form a coherent statement.
O: population is expected to triple in
P: the next 50 years
Q: among the world’s poorest countries
R: population shrinkage in that period
S: whereas many rich countries will see
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. QOPSR.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct sequence is: (Q) among the world's poorest countries (O) population is expected to triple in (P) the next 50 years (S) whereas many rich countries will see (R) population shrinkage in that period, forming: "Among the world's poorest countries, population is expected to triple in the next 50 years, whereas many rich countries will see population shrinkage in that period."

• Q opens the sentence, setting up the group being discussed ("among the world's poorest countries"), which needs a following clause about what happens to them.

• O and P together complete the first half of the sentence describing the population trend and its time frame ("population is expected to triple in the next 50 years").

• S introduces the contrasting second half with "whereas", and R completes it, describing the opposite trend ("population shrinkage") occurring "in that period" — a phrase that refers back to "the next 50 years" established earlier.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: POSQR is incorrect because it opens with "the next 50 years" (P) with no preceding clause for this time phrase to attach to, producing a disjointed opening.

• Option 2: RSOPQ is incorrect because it opens with "population shrinkage in that period" (R), but the phrase "that period" has no antecedent yet defined, making the reference unclear.

• Option 3: SPORQ is incorrect because it opens with "whereas many rich countries will see" (S), but a sentence cannot logically begin with a contrast conjunction like "whereas" before the first idea it is meant to contrast with has been stated.

NOTE

• In segment-rearrangement questions with a "whereas"/"while" contrast structure, the first idea (here, poor countries' population growth) must always be stated before the "whereas" clause introducing the second, contrasting idea.

• Watch for phrases like "that period" or "this reason" which require an antecedent to have already appeared earlier in the sequence.

question:
Select the option that expresses the following sentence in active voice.
The car was repaired by the mechanic.
option_2: The mechanic has repaired the car.
option_3: The mechanic is repairing the car.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. The mechanic repaired the car.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "The car was repaired by the mechanic" is in the Simple Past Tense (passive voice).

• Rule — Simple Past Tense:
◦ Passive: Object + was/were + V3 + by + Subject
◦ Active: Subject + V2 + Object

• Applying the rule: the agent "the mechanic" becomes the subject; the past participle "repaired" becomes the simple past verb "repaired" (V2, same form here since "repair" is a regular verb); and "the car" becomes the object.
◦ Active: The mechanic repaired the car.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "repairs" is the Simple Present Tense form, which changes the time frame of the original past-tense sentence.

• Option 2 is incorrect because "has repaired" is the Present Perfect Tense form, not the Simple Past Tense required to match the original sentence.

• Option 3 is incorrect because "is repairing" is the Present Continuous Tense form, again shifting the time frame away from the simple past.

NOTE

• A quick check for active-passive conversion questions: first identify the tense of the given (passive) sentence precisely, then apply only that tense's active-voice formula — never assume Simple Past just because "by" is used.

• Regular verbs like "repair" have identical V2 (simple past) and V3 (past participle) forms — "repaired" — which can make such questions look deceptively similar; always confirm by checking the auxiliary verb used in the passive sentence.

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Appearances may not reveal the man. So, you shouldn’t make (1)________ about a man’s character based on how he (2)________ . People smile and smile, yet prove to be (3)________ . On the other hand, people with rough exteriors prove to be the (4)________ and most considerate people on earth. They are the people who are beautiful from (5)________ .

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.(
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. assumptions.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank requires a noun meaning "things believed to be true without proof," matching the sense of judging someone's character without real evidence. "Assumptions" means things taken for granted or believed without verification, which exactly fits "you shouldn't make assumptions about a man's character."

• Rule: In cloze-passage questions, the chosen word must form a natural collocation with the surrounding words — here, the fixed expression is "to make assumptions (about something)", a common collocation in English.

• Applying the rule: "you shouldn't make assumptions about a man's character based on how he looks" completes the sentence both grammatically and logically, continuing the passage's theme that appearances can be misleading.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "ascend" means to climb or rise; it is a verb, not a noun that collocates with "make", and is unrelated in meaning to judging character.

• Option 2: "derivations" means the process of obtaining something from a source, or the origin of a word; it does not fit the sense of forming a hasty judgement about someone.

• Option 3: "deficient" is an adjective meaning lacking something; it cannot grammatically follow "make" as a noun object here, and does not fit the intended meaning.

NOTE

• Common fixed collocations with "make" tested by SSC: make an assumption, make a decision, make an effort, make a mistake, make progress.

• The passage's central theme — "don't judge a book by its cover" — is a commonly tested idiom carrying the same idea as this cloze passage.

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Appearances may not reveal the man. So, you shouldn’t make (1)________ about a man’s character based on how he (2)________ . People smile and smile, yet prove to be (3)________ . On the other hand, people with rough exteriors prove to be the (4)________ and most considerate people on earth. They are the people who are beautiful from (5)________ .

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 2.(
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. looks.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank requires a verb describing physical appearance, following "based on how he ___". "Looks" means appears or seems in outward appearance, which correctly completes "based on how he looks" — i.e., based on his physical/outward appearance.

• Rule: In cloze passages, the verb chosen must agree grammatically with the subject ("he", third person singular, requiring "-s") and must fit the logical topic of the sentence — here, the topic is judging a man's character by his outward appearance.

• Applying the rule: "you shouldn't make assumptions about a man's character based on how he looks" correctly conveys that outward appearance should not determine judgement of character, consistent with the rest of the passage.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "admits" means to confess or acknowledge something; it does not fit the sense of physical appearance intended here.

• Option 2: "shows" means to display or reveal; while related to appearance, it does not idiomatically follow "based on how he ___" in the way "looks" does, and shifts the intended meaning to an active display rather than outward appearance.

• Option 3: "glitters" means to shine with a bright, sparkling light; it is used for physical shininess of objects, not for describing a person's general appearance in this context.

NOTE

• The verb "look" used intransitively (as here, "how he looks") means "to appear/seem", distinct from "look at" (to direct one's gaze) — a commonly tested distinction.

• The passage's logic pairs with the well-known saying "Looks can be deceiving," reinforcing why "looks" is the natural fit here.

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Appearances may not reveal the man. So, you shouldn’t make (1)________ about a man’s character based on how he (2)________ . People smile and smile, yet prove to be (3)________ . On the other hand, people with rough exteriors prove to be the (4)________ and most considerate people on earth. They are the people who are beautiful from (5)________ .

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 3.(
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. grumpy.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank requires a word that creates a contrast with "smile and smile," fitting the passage's central theme that outward appearance and inward character can be opposite. "Grumpy" means bad-tempered and irritable, which creates exactly the ironic contrast intended: people who smile constantly on the outside may actually be ill-tempered on the inside.

• Rule: In cloze passages built around a specific theme (here, the contrast between appearance and reality), the correct blank-filler must sustain that theme's logic rather than merely fitting the sentence grammatically.

• Applying the rule: "People smile and smile, yet prove to be grumpy" completes the irony that a constant smile does not guarantee a good temperament, matching the passage's later statement that rough-looking people can, in contrast, be "the kindest".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "ecstatic" means extremely happy or joyful; this would agree with, not contrast, the idea of smiling, so it breaks the passage's ironic logic (the word "yet" signals a contrast is needed).

• Option 3: "joyful" similarly means full of happiness, again agreeing with "smile" rather than contrasting with it, which does not fit after the contrast-word "yet".

• Option 4: "sparkling" means shining brightly, or (of a person) vivacious and lively; like "ecstatic" and "joyful", it aligns with rather than contrasts the idea of smiling, so it fails to fit the sentence's contrastive structure signalled by "yet".

NOTE

• The word "yet" here functions as a contrast connector (similar to "but" or "however") — always check for such connectors in cloze passages, as they signal that the blank must oppose, not agree with, the preceding idea.

• This passage echoes the popular theme of "not judging a book by its cover," commonly tested through cloze/reading-comprehension passages in SSC exams.

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Appearances may not reveal the man. So, you shouldn’t make (1)________ about a man’s character based on how he (2)________ . People smile and smile, yet prove to be (3)________ . On the other hand, people with rough exteriors prove to be the (4)________ and most considerate people on earth. They are the people who are beautiful from (5)________ .

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 4.(
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. kindest.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank requires a superlative adjective that pairs naturally with "and most considerate," describing people with rough exteriors in a positive light. "Kindest" means most kind, gentle, and generous in nature, which fits perfectly alongside "most considerate" to describe such people positively.

• Rule: In cloze passages, when a blank is joined to another descriptive word by "and" (here, "the ___ and most considerate people"), both words must belong to the same positive or negative category — since "most considerate" is clearly positive, the blank must also be a positive superlative.

• Applying the rule: "people with rough exteriors prove to be the kindest and most considerate people on earth" completes the passage's ironic contrast — those who look tough on the outside are, in fact, the gentlest and most caring on the inside.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "bitterest" means most resentful or harsh; this is a negative quality, which contradicts the clearly positive "most considerate" it is paired with.

• Option 2: "strangest" means most odd or unusual; this is a neutral/negative descriptor unrelated to kindness, and does not pair sensibly with "most considerate".

• Option 3: "gloomiest" means most sad or dark in mood; this too is a negative quality, which clashes with the positive tone required alongside "most considerate".

NOTE

• When two descriptive words are joined by "and" in a sentence, they are almost always of the same positive/negative polarity — a useful check in cloze/fill-in-the-blank questions.

• The passage's message reinforces the common saying that "appearances can be deceptive," a theme frequently used as the basis for SSC reading/cloze passages.

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Appearances may not reveal the man. So, you shouldn’t make (1)________ about a man’s character based on how he (2)________ . People smile and smile, yet prove to be (3)________ . On the other hand, people with rough exteriors prove to be the (4)________ and most considerate people on earth. They are the people who are beautiful from (5)________ .

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 5.(
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. within.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank completes the phrase **"beautiful from ___", and "within" means on the inside; internally, giving the fixed, idiomatic expression "beautiful from within"** — meaning a person's true beauty lies in their inner character, not outward appearance.

• Rule: Cloze-passage blanks at the end of a passage often complete a well-known idiomatic phrase; recognising such fixed expressions ("beautiful from within", "rotten to the core", etc.) is key to choosing the correct filler.

• Applying the rule: "They are the people who are beautiful from within" neatly closes the passage's argument that true beauty/goodness is internal (character), not based on external appearance — tying back to the opening line, "Appearances may not reveal the man."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "personality" does not fit the fixed phrase "beautiful from ___"; saying "beautiful from personality" is not idiomatic or grammatically natural English.

• Option 3: "style" similarly does not fit; "beautiful from style" is not a recognised or meaningful expression in this context.

• Option 4: "exterior" would directly contradict the passage's argument — the whole point is that true beauty is NOT about the "exterior" (outward appearance) but about one's inner nature, so this option reverses the intended meaning.

NOTE

• The idiomatic phrase "beautiful from within" is commonly used to mean that inner character/goodness matters more than physical appearance — a frequently tested vocabulary/comprehension concept.

• The passage as a whole reflects the well-known theme "Don't judge a book by its cover," reinforcing that outward appearance can be misleading about a person's true character.
